Method · as of 4 November 2026

Freeze, measure once, count.

A reading that “makes sense” does not prove a key: with enough freedom, numbers can be made to say anything. So before attacking a cipher we write down what we will measure and what will count as success. Then we measure once, on a passage the key has never seen, and we publish the result, failures included.

Method of Brice Dudout, applied with Claude agents · this page describes our working rules, not those of other researchers · the computing tools stay private: the method is described here, the code is not published

In short

  1. Prior work first. Before working, and again before publishing, we check whether the text has already been read: printed editions, Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, the DECODE database, Cryptiana, period decipherments.
  2. A written, hashed protocol. Training data, the held-out passage, the measurement and the thresholds are written in a file whose SHA-256 fingerprint is recorded before any attempt.
  3. A key learned, then frozen. The key comes from cipher/plain pairs (period decipherment, clear copy) or from probable words; it is then frozen and hashed.
  4. One measurement. The frozen key deciphers the held-out passage; the score is compared with the best of 200 shuffled keys. The thresholds are those of the protocol, not those one would like afterwards.
  5. A count, not an impression. The reading is counted word by word (sure, probable, restored, unresolved), following Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: at least 95% before calling it a decipherment.
  6. Everything is published, failures included, with an explicit class: already known, partial or new.

First: who has read it already?

Many “unsolved” ciphers were solved long ago: the plaintext sits in a nineteenth-century edition, in a neighbouring volume, or between the lines of the document itself. Before attacking, we therefore check, in this order:

  • the document and its file: period decipherment between the lines or in the margin, clear copy, draft, deciphered duplicate;
  • printed editions: published correspondence, calendars, document collections, nunciature editions; a clear sentence next to the cipher is often enough to find the edition;
  • Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (cyphersolver): catalogue, leads, open targets, pending requests and contributions;
  • DECODE: the record’s status (deciphered or not) and decipherments already deposited;
  • Satoshi Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana and recent literature (Cryptologia, HistoCrypt).

The check is repeated before publication. It is never exhaustive, and we say so: at Dole, the 1912 printed edition was found only after the reading; the card says so, and the comparison with the print is presented as a confirmation, not as a control. When someone else publishes the same reading on the same day, both readings are published and each cites the other (Puebla’s letter of 1506, read in parallel by WAINUT).

A frozen, hashed protocol

Every attack starts with a PROTOCOLE file, written before looking at the part that will serve as control. It fixes:

  • the training pages or lines, and the held-out passage (H), with what we have already seen of it (often nothing, sometimes a thumbnail);
  • the normalisation of the reference plaintext (lower case, u/v and i/j merged, accents removed);
  • how the key will be learned and frozen;
  • the measurement, the control, the random seed and the thresholds for success, partial reading and failure;
  • what will be done if the key is validated, and what will not be done if it fails.

The protocol, the transcription and the frozen key are hashed with SHA-256 and their fingerprints recorded before the measurement. Anyone can thus check afterwards that none of these files was retouched to obtain the result.

Amendments. A parameter error found along the way is corrected by a dated amendment, hashed as well, and only before the measurement. Example: for the second Dole cipher, the learned alignment declared every number a “null”; noticed on the training data alone, the cost of a null was raised from 2 to 4.5 by an amendment, before the held-out block was deciphered. After the measurement nothing changes: a new idea needs a new protocol and a new held-out passage, never a second try on the same one.

Building the key

We mostly read chancery ciphers from the sixteenth to the twentieth century: homophonic substitutions, nomenclators, numerical codes, grids. The key is built in three ways, from the safest to the least safe.

  1. Learning from cipher/plain pairs. Period offices often deciphered part of the letters, between the lines or in the margin; a clear copy of the same letter may exist. These pairs are the training data: for each sign, the most frequent value in the alignment. Rare signs are completed by a structural rule observed on the training data (alphabetical order of the table, homophones grouped by three, and so on), stated in the protocol.
  2. Using an existing key. A period table kept elsewhere, a key printed or published by another researcher (Tomokiyo, Bourdeau, Meister…). It is then cited, and what is measured is its application to our document.
  3. Attacking with probable words. With no plaintext at all, we start from what the context makes likely: forms of address, dates, names mentioned in the nearby clear text, repeated words. A word hypothesis fixes a few values, which must hold everywhere else; a solver then completes the rest. Passages used to place these words can no longer serve as the held-out passage.

Before letters, we look at structure: number of distinct signs, group length, separators, probable nulls, the order of the table. It often tells us which family of key to look for, and it avoids fitting a simple substitution to a code that is not one.

The single measurement: hold-out, control, thresholds

The frozen key deciphers the held-out passage mechanically: an unknown sign stays unknown (“?”), no word is corrected by hand. The output is compared with the reference plaintext of the held-out passage (period decipherment, clear copy).

  • “Characters” score: share of letters rendered correctly.
  • M5 score: share of words of five letters or more rendered exactly. It penalises errors more severely.
  • Control: the values of the key are shuffled at random between the signs, 200 times (seed recorded), and the same measurement is repeated; we keep the best of the 200. The control says what a wrong key of the same shape obtains by chance on this text.
VerdictCondition (fixed before the measurement)
Key validatedcharacters ≥ 0.85 and at least 0.30 above the best control; or M5 ≥ 0.60
Partialat least 0.30 above the best control, without reaching the absolute threshold
Failureanything else

A partial key is not a validated key: its text is not published as a decipherment. The held-out passage is measured only once: once deciphered, it is “used up”, even if the score disappoints.

These thresholds have been common to our dossiers since late October 2026. The first cards (October) were checked with other measurements, stated in each: distance in standard deviations over 2,000 permuted keys (Duplessis-Mornay, 1593), quadgram likelihood against 1,000 controls (Nisa, 1644), share of recognised words against permuted keys (Charles XII, 1710). We leave them as they were made, without recomputing them afterwards.

Reading: the “read by sense” count

A validated key is not enough: every word still has to be read. We count the reading by Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: a text is “read” when at least 95% of the cipher words are read by sense. Each word gets a status:

  • sure: the frozen transcription gives the word as it stands;
  • probable {x}: a doubtful letter, an overwritten sign, a value seen only once;
  • restored by sense [x]: the word is missing or illegible and the context requires it;
  • unresolved ‹…›: not read, and left visible in the text.

The 95% threshold is computed on the sure and probable words, without the restored ones: a rate that owes much to restorations is not worth the same. We also give, in brackets, the rate with the restored words. Since 4 November 2026 this rule applies to every card: those that passed the threshold only with the restored words have become partial readings. The count is redone mechanically by a script on the published text, not estimated by hand. Below 95%, the card is an explained partial reading: we say how many words are missing, where, and why (binding, ink, nomenclator not found).

Blind re-reading

Most uncertainties come from the transcription: one dot more or less, two similar shapes. To settle them without being led by the expected word, we prepare re-reading sheets:

  • a single sign framed per question, in its graphic context;
  • the possible answers are thumbnails of shapes by the same hand, cut elsewhere in the document from sure words, with no value or interpretation shown; plus “none” and “illegible”, and a free remark;
  • neutral identifiers, shuffled questions and options; the mapping between thumbnails and values is kept outside the page;
  • the list of questions is written and hashed (PREREG) before the sheet is built; a question whose frame misses its sign is withdrawn, never moved to another word;
  • the sheet is tested before it is handed over; Brice Dudout answers it, and the recount is then made from the exported answers.

Sheets cover only the doubtful signs and their immediate neighbours: they are not a second full reading. Their effect is published in the card (for the Huguenot memorandum of about 1583, for instance, 527 sure and 102 probable words before, 533 and 96 after).

Classifying the result

Each card states at the outset what was known and what is new.

ClassMeaningWhat we claim
existingthe plaintext existed: period decipherment, printed edition, reading published by someone elseat most the key, the identification of a piece, a verification or corrections; never the “solution”
partialpartial key, or reading below 95%an explained partial reading, with its gaps counted
newvalidated key and a reading of at least 95%, with no known plaintext to our knowledgea first published decipherment, “to our knowledge”

We also state how the key was obtained, using the vocabulary of Daniel Bourdeau’s repository: from ciphertext only, from a plaintext found elsewhere, from adjacent plaintext in the same file, by matching an existing key, by applying a known key, or from an existing decipherment. A reading redone after another researcher goes on the Independent checks page, with its priority.

One example, one failure: Dole, 1636

During the siege of Dole, the Parlement and Antoine Brun wrote to the relief army in a “dotted” cipher: one number per letter. The letters received are in Besançon (dossier Dole, 1636).

  • Training: the first cipher block of f. 200, deciphered in the margin by a period hand (177 numbers for 177 letters).
  • Held-out: the second block of the same folio (341 numbers), with its gloss, chosen before the attack.
  • Single measurement: 0.907 of letters correct; best of 200 controls 0.229 (mean 0.131). Both thresholds are met: key validated.
  • Reading of the passages without gloss: 128 words, 113 sure, 11 probable, 4 unresolved, i.e. 96.9%.
  • Class: the text had been in print since 1912 (Émile Longin), found afterwards. The key is our contribution; the text is “existing”.

The failure, published in the same dossier. In August the besieged changed cipher (f. 106, 78 numbers, a 63-letter gloss). Same procedure, held-out passage taken from the same piece for want of another letter, a limit stated in the protocol. Measurement: 0.160, below the best control (0.280). Failure: the block is too short and the system is probably not a simple substitution. We did not try another held-out passage on the same block.

Two partial readings. The Duke of Sessa to Charles V (1524) reads at 93.0% (94.0% with the restored words): fourteen words short of the threshold, and the card says so. The letter of the Electors of Mainz and Cologne (1633) reads at 84.2% and could not exceed 91.4%: nineteen words are lost in the binding. Elsewhere, a key measured at 0.778 against 0.417 for the best control (a gap of 0.36, but below 0.85) stayed “partial”: its reading is not published.

Images and licences

We reproduce an archival image only if it is in the public domain or under an explicit open licence (Public Domain Mark, CC BY…), with the credit requested: for example NARA, the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, the Real Academia de la Historia, the Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv, old editions on Internet Archive, Wikimedia Commons. Facsimiles from Gallica (BnF) are reproduced under its terms for non-commercial reuse, with the credit “Source gallica.bnf.fr / BnF” under each image.

Never reproduced, whether as thumbnail, crop or derivative: images from DECODE (provided for research and transcription only), the Biblioteca Nacional de España, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, the Besançon library (Mémoire vive), the Hohenlohe-Zentralarchiv, the Hessisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, JACAR, the Austrian State Archives, the ANTT and the Rigsarkivet. We give the shelfmark and a link to the record. A reading based on a DECODE record cites it as “DECODE Rn”, with a link to the record. An automatic check prevents the publication of any image registered as coming from DECODE.

AI-generated atmosphere illustrations are labelled as such and never serve as sources.

Who does what, and credits

The work. Transcriptions, key learning, measurements and counts are done by Claude agents, directed by Brice Dudout, who chooses the dossiers, answers the re-reading sheets and decides each publication. The computing tools are kept in a private repository; the method is described here, the code is not published.

Credits. A result due to others is credited by name, in the card and in the sources: Daniel Bourdeau (the cyphersolver catalogue, leads, tables, the 95% rule), Satoshi Tomokiyo (Cryptiana, reconstructed tables, earlier readings), George Lasry (published readings and keys), WAINUT (leads and parallel readings), Ilia Chirtulov (King Joseph’s letter, 1812), the DECODE database, and the archives that hold the documents. A key already in print is not ours: we cite it. Each result published here is also offered to Daniel Bourdeau’s repository, with its exact role (solution, partial reading, verification, corrected key, lead).

Limits and published failures

  • One reader. Signs are read from images, often by a single reader, sometimes from microfilm; blind re-reading covers only the doubtful signs.
  • Short held-out passages. When no other piece exists, the held-out passage is taken from the same document as the training data, and may have fewer than a hundred signs: the protocol says so.
  • What the control does not say. The control rules out chance, not a nearly right neighbouring key; it does not replace word-by-word reading.
  • Conventional thresholds. 0.85, 0.30, 0.60 and 95% are conventions chosen in advance; a document may be well understood just below the threshold, and it then stays “partial”.
  • Prior-work checks are never exhaustive. An old edition may escape us; we correct the card as soon as it is pointed out.
  • Failures stay online: the August 1636 cipher at Dole, Biglia’s first letter (94.5%, not published), the partial readings of Longlée (1590), Sessa (1524), the Electors (1633), part of Sega’s letter (1590), and eight cards that became partial readings when the 95% rule was applied without the restored words (4 November 2026).

Appendix: the Medici dossier (October 2026)

The site’s first dossier, the two letters of Marie de’ Medici to Brèves (1610), was read before this protocol was set: by a manual sign-by-sign alignment, with no held-out passage and no control. We keep its decisions here as they were taken.

The key and its homophones

The reading matches the signs with a table in manuscript Français 3462, frame 112 (Gallica record): several signs for one letter, values for syllables or words, numbers and nulls.[3] The identifiers A1, A2… denote the homophones in column A, from top to bottom; a single value is kept per sign.

Reading the key in practice

Shapes must be compared, not letters typed on a keyboard: D1 and S3 are two different signs despite a rough transcription as “t”. The nomenclator adds units of variable length: a, → ce, x, → en, y, → et, 4 → Sa Sainteté, 41~ → leurs. A single merge is documented: tu = U3 (99 former boxes, 98 edited glyphs). Images and notes are in card f17 L2.

Four corroborated values

Four values first proposed from context received the support of Satoshi Tomokiyo on 17 October 2026. This support concerns the numerical values, not the full identity of Marie’s key.[7]

Overlined codeValueOccurrences
72~que2
79~re1
86~se2
90~tion1

Leads and experiments

Before the retained reading, several leads failed or remained explorations: a longer sister letter (another piece), the alphabet read in blocks (no running French), the first survey of the table (alphabet misread), table constraints and probable words (risk of overfitting). These attempts are not independent controls of the final reading.

Three levels of checking

Re-reading of the shapes against the table; re-examination of eight points in context (three possible, five undecidable); the expert opinion of Satoshi Tomokiyo, who had seen our proposal: an opinion, not a blind experiment.

What remains probable

The general sense is very likely, but the text is not solved to the character: eight points remain undecidable or possible, and the ending LEUR/LEURS remains open. Without a measurement on a held-out passage, this dossier would not be classed today as a “validated key”: it is a proposed reading.
